sections.heading: Aurangabad- Monument- Kailasanatha Temple at Ellora
sections.content: A marvel of engineering and artistry Kailasanatha temple dates back to the period of the eight century Rashtrakuta period. It is a collosal monolithic rock cut temple built in the Dravidian style and is known for its architectural grandeur as well as its sculptural splendour. More than thirty temples have been carved from the hillside at Ellora during the period sixth to ninth centuries CE. Its excavation must rank as an architectural wonder. Two great trenches some ninety meters long were dug into the hillside. They were connected at the deepest point by another trench fifty three metres across. The temple was meant to appear as though rising from a vast courtyard at ground level. The great block of residual rock, rising thirty metres, was then carved into the three- storeyed vimana, the main mandapa, two giant dhwajasthambas or pillars, and four sub- shrines. Beginning at the top, the mass of rock was hewn into shape, and as each layer was shaped, the carvers began ornamenting the structure moving downward, thus eliminating the need for any scaffolding. The temple is dedicated to Shiva and named after his abode in the Himalayas, the Kailasa. It was built during the period 757 and 773 CE. The temple covers a large area and the vimana (tower) rises to a height of about ninety feet. The most amazing thing to be emphasized over and over again and seen to be believed is that the entire monument was made by excavation and not by construction. The typical Dravidian features includes a gateway, an enclosure for the Nandi, and a mandapa lined up in front of the sanctum which is crowned with a vimana, composed of successively receding storeys, decroated with miniature buildings. The mandapa in front of the sanctum is an enormous pillared hall with elaborate carving. On either side of the Nandi mandapa are two fifty feet high obelisk like pillars decorated with frieze carvings. Two storeys of corridors have been carved into the mountain, ringing the temple on three sides. These corridors are studded with small alcoves, all containing a wealth of sculpted figures telling the tales of the great Hindu epics, the Mahabharata and the Ramayana. Among the narrative friezes is the descent of river Ganga, and one of Ravana shaking Mount Kailasa. The architectural style and intricate sculpture is similar to Virupaksha Temple at Pattadakal that had been completed a decade before. A collonaded gallery running along the bottom of the cliff face forms a deep narrow passage that surrounds the temple. In between this cliff face and the temple is the pradakshinapatha. The temple tower resembles the rathas at Mamallapuram near Chennai in Tamilnadu. The Kailasanatha temple resembles the architectural style established by the Pallavas of Mamallapuram and is yet considerably grander in scale. Other caves of interest in Ellora are the Rameshwar cave, the Sita ki Nahani cave, and several Jain caves such as the Indra Sabha cave, all dating back to the period of sixth-ninth centuries CE.

sections.heading: Mumbai- Monument- Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus (formerly Victoria Terminus)
sections.content: The Chhatrapati Shivaji terminus, formerly known as Victoria Terminus in Mumbai was designed by Frederick William Stevens. It is an outstanding example of Victorian Gothic architecture in India, blended with themes deriving from Indian traditional architecture. The terminal was built over ten years starting in 1878 according to a design based on late medieval Italian models. Its remarkable stone dome, turrets, pointed arches, and interesting ground plan are close to traditional Indian palace architecture. The interiors are adorned with wood carving, tiles, ornamental iron and brass railings, grills for the ticket offices, and the grand staircase with balustrades.

sections.heading: Mumbai- Monument- Gateway of India
sections.content: The Gateway of India, a massive archway on the Apollo Bunder, is one of the grand and magnificent landmarks of Mumbai, which was built to commemorate the visit of the British Monarch, King George V and Queen Mary. The Gateway of India is one of the hot spots of Mumbai city. Designed by the architect George Wittet it was formally opened in 1924 by the then Viceroy, Earl of Reading. The Gateway is a 26m high structure with four turrets and complicated lattice work engraved into the yellow basalt stone. The central dome of the Gateway of India is 48 feet in diameter. It is interesting to note that the whole harbour front was realligned in order to come in line with a planned walkway, sweeping down to the centre of the town. At the back of the Gateway arch, steps lead down to the sea front.

sections.heading: Mumbai- Monument- Elephanta
sections.content: The Elephanta Island is located ten km away from the Gateway of India at Mumbai. These caves house rock cut temples dating back to the fifth century CE. Elephanta Island was so named by the Portuguese, after the statue of an elephant near the landing area of the island. There are six caves dating back to sixth and seventh century. These rock cut temples dedicated to Lord Shiva are abundant in sculptural content. Created by carving out rocks, and creating columns, internal spaces and the images, the entire temple can be compared to a huge sculpture. Some of the rock surfaces are highly finished while some are untreated bare rock. The entire cave temple consists of a main chamber and two lateral ones, courtyards and several subsidiary shrines. Above the temple is the mass of natural rock. There are three entrances to this temple with the one on the east and the west marking the axis of the temple. A twenty pillared hall lines the axis, and on its western end is the cella in which is enshrined a Shiva linga. The pillars consist of fluted columns standing on square bases, and are crowned with fluted cushioned capitals. The most enigmatic image is of Trimurti or the Sadasiva manifestation of Shiva which is a collossal twenty feet high image of the three headed Shiva. Also on the southern wall are grand sculptured images of Kalyanasundara, Gangadhara, Ardhanariswara and Uma Maheswara. To the west of the northern entrance are sculptured images of Nataraja and Andhakaasuravadha urth, and to its east are images of Yogiswara and Ravanaanugrahamurthy in eight manifest forms. At Elephanta caves, Shiva is portrayed in the non-anthropomorphic Shivalinga form, as well as in the colossal human image. The secondary shrine is located to the east of the main temple in a courtyard. This temple contains six pillars at its entrance, four of which are free standing and two connected. The entrance leads to a hall decorated with sculptured panels depicting legends from the Shiva Purana.

sections.heading: Aurangabad- Monument- Bibi Ka Makbara
sections.content: Bibi Ka Maqbara, the burial place of Aurangzeb's 1st wife, Rabia-ud-Durrani is an imitation of the Taj at Agra and is often referred to as the poor mans Taj Mahal due to its poor copy of the masterpiece. The mausoleum is made mostly of sandstone and has plastered walls and a marble dome.The tomb is adornedwith lattice work in marble and inlay decorations of flowers and creepers which are beautiful. A high wall with bastions runs around the monument and the recesses have little minarets. The entrance leads to an arch and from this point, a fine view of the structure ahead may be obtained. The pavement that leads to the mausoleum is flanked by oblong reservoirs.

sections.heading: Daulatabad Fort
sections.content: Once known as Devagiri, this place was later renamed as Daulatabad by the then Sultan of Delhi, Mohammed - bin - Tughlak. One of the world's best preserved forts of medieval times the fort has hundreds of secret passages. The fortress was built to be secure with three massive walls to defend it against enemy attacks. The fort has some impressive structures like the Chand Minar, Jami Masjid and Royal Palace which are worth mentioning. The palace also has a few spacious halls, courtyards and pavilions.

sections.heading: Mumbai- Monument- Kanheri Cave
sections.content: Kanheri caves were the viharas for the Buddhist monks during the period between second century BCE and ninth century CE. These caves are simple and bare, quite different from that of Elephanta caves which are artistically embellished. Kanheri caves are mostly tiny cells that are cut into the edges of a hill, each having a stone plinth that might have served as a bed. There is also a congregation hall supported by huge stone pillars that contains the dagoba, a kind of Buddhist shrine. The largest is the Cave 13 which is adorned with sculptures in front of the stupa.

sections.heading: Lonavla- Monument- Bhaja Cave
sections.content: The Bhaja caves near Lonavla are the perfect examples of the phase of early Buddhist architecture. Lord Buddha has been represented here through numerous symbols in the caves. However, the caves which were carved after the fourth century CE, also presents the Buddha in his physical forms. The pillars of these caves are carved with figures of flowers and other images. The cave 12, is a Chaitya hall, which is the largest of all has a fine vault. The last cave towards the south is a good example of fine architecture and sculpture. This cave includes the figures of a dancing couple, a prince seated on an elephant and The remaining 7 caves contain inscriptions about the donors. The chaitya caves do not have a wall in the front as they are open which might have been enclosed by a wooden door of some kind in olden days. The patterns of the ceilings are prototypes of wooden ceilings.

sections.heading: Karle- Monument- Karle Cave
sections.content: The Buddhist caves at Karle, built by the Buddhist monks, are the epitome of ancient rock-cut caves to be found in India. Dating back from the second to first century BCE, the Karle caves in Lonavla, were built during the Satvahahana period and hosted the monks in the monsoons, Built from top to bottom in the form of a ladder, the early Karle caves do not depict the Buddha in his physical forms but rather in symbols. However, from the seventh century CE when the Mahayana became more popular with their liberal thoughts, the later Karle caves do present the Buddha in his physical form such as the Buddha preaching while seated on a lion-supported throne, along withother magnificent carvings. The caves comprise mainly two types of structures: chaitya halls and viharas. The chaitya halls, which form the largest number of chaityas in the world (one being one hundred and forty eight feet long), were used for congregational worship whereas the viharas were the dwelling place for the monks and further included cells cut into the walls around three sides of a hall used for their residential and individual meditation. The pillars of the halls inside the caves have been carved with figures of men, women, flowers and elephants, though the pillars outside these halls have lions erected on them as their crowns, an emblem of Ashoka, the great Indian ruler.

sections.heading: Warli Paintings
sections.content: Warli painting derives its name from a tribe living in the remote regions of Maharashtra. Their imagination, beliefs and customs are freely and spontaneously expressed in their monochromatic paintings. The walls of the village of Warli have been adorned with these paintings for centuries and even today they form the primary decoration in most of the houses. Their way of life, trees, birds, men and women form composite paintings, and the most joyous celebration of their life. The moods of their life make for interesting themes, which is why Warli paintings are much more than designs on walls; they are authentic depictions of a way of life. The Warlis live in thatched mud-huts, which are constructed in such a way so that they all surround a central common area. They are primarily an agriculture-dependant tribe. Historians believe that the Warli tradition can be traced back to the neolithic period between 2500 BCE and 3000 BCE. During the harvest season, and weddings and births, their houses are adorned with a variety of patterns. The Warli way of life is beautifully captured in simple images in white against earthen background. Geometric designs dominate most paintings; dots and crooked lines are the units of these compositions. Spiral formations of men and women and concentric circular designs are symbolic of these paintings. The harmony and balance depicted in these paintings is supposed to signify the harmony and balance of the universe. Marriage is the most common theme of Warli paintings. Many paintings have a depiction of Palghat, the marriage God, accompanied by a horse and of course the bride and the groom. These paintings are sacred and without them the marriage cannot take place. Men and women in spirals dancing in celebration, is another theme typical to the Warli paintings. A musician playing a native instrument is usually found in the middle of such spirals. Flora and fauna are also depicted in these paintings.

sections.heading: Mumbai- Museum- Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya (Prince of Wales Museum)
sections.content: Some prominent citizens of Bombay decided to set up a Museum with the help of the government to commemorate the Prince of Wales, the Crown Prince who visited Bombay in 1905 and later became King George V, who laid the foundation stone of the museum. The exquisite basalt stone structure with its large central dome inspired by the Bijapur domes and beautiful gardens are set in a crescent shaped piece of land. Art, archaeology and natural history are three exclusive sections in the museum. It houses some of the finest collections, ranging from ancient Indus Valley relics to the artifacts from the Gupta and Maurya Periods. Here, one can see a few of the rarest and earliest exhibits of Indian history. There are scores of interesting artifacts from foreign countries like Tibet and Nepal. It has one complete gallery comprising the exquisite thangka scrolls of the Buddhists. Another gallery is devoted to bronze castings and stone sculptures and more than 2,000 miniature paintings from the different styles and phases of India. The collection presents the evolution of painting in India, ranging between eleventh and twelveth century illustrated palm leaf manuscripts to early nineteenth century Pahari paintings. Exquisite examples of all the main schools of miniature painting are on view, Rajput, Mughal, Pahari, and Deccani, each school with its characteristic style has its own delicacy of form and colour. The variety of art displayed in the museum is definitely a treat for any art-lover.

sections.heading: The Raja Dinkar Kelkar Museum
sections.content: Dr. Dinkar Kelkar started collecting artifacts and objects around 1920s and by the sixties he had accumulated around 15000 exhibits. He was a great lover of Indian art. The Kelkar Museum is the result of his tireless efforts of about sixty years. It is a museum with a collection of everyday objects like pots, lamps, containers, nutcrackers, pen stands etc. Objects have been classified according to their materials and techniques of making them and their function. There are some unique collections in this museum. There is an assortment of oil lamps made of different materials right from clay to brass, each with their own shape and form and usage right from rituals, to practical lighting.Some beautiful, intricately carved wooden doors and windows adorn the museum. They are collected from Gujarat, Rajasthan, Karnataka and Kerala. Another kind of collection is of locks used for both trunks and doors. They are of interesting shapes of dogs, horses and even scorpions. One remarkable collection is the chitakathi scroll paintings which tell us the great tradition of the village storyteller and accompaniment of music and song.

sections.heading: Maharashtra- Handicrafts- Kolhapuri Chappals
sections.content: Kohlapuri chappals are handcrafted leather sandals that get their name from the place of their origin, the district of Kohlapur. Intricate patterns are handcrafted and made of leather; the interesting fact is that even the cords used to stitch the sandals are made of leather and no nails are used. The hide of bulls, cows, and goats are used for the leather. Kachkadi, bakkalnali, and pukari are some traditional designs. Kohlapuri chappals range from those with simple straps and plain colours and designs to more decorative ones with a gold cord or gota on them. These chappals, which were probably worn only by the inhabitants of Kohlapur, are now worn all over India and abroad.

sections.heading: Maharashtra- Handicrafts- Lacquerware
sections.content: Savantvadi in Ratnagiri district is famous for its unique, brightly coloured lacquered toys and dolls, imitation fruits and vegetables. The best known is a set with a man and a woman and a toy winnowing fan in folk style. They mainly show men and women in either standing or sitting postures. Hale and pangora wood is used by the traditional craftsmen who are known as chittorees (picture makers). At one time this was a big craft centre for the round lacquered highly pictorial playing cards known as ganjifa.

sections.heading: Maharashtra- Handicrafts- Paithani Silk Sarees
sections.content: A very beautiful style of saree called paithani named after the village Paithan is a well known handicraft of Maharashtra. On a zari wrap thread the weft is interlocked with different colours. In this technique, complicated patterns of flowers and birds are woven in bright colours. Asavali (vine and flowers), Narli (coconut design) and petal design are the few traditional motifs. Due to the closeness of Paithan to the famous Ajanta caves, there are motifs of Buddha woven standing or in the sitting posture and motifs of gold coins are also represented in the weaves. The pallu is an exquisite piece of gold tissue around which are woven brightly coloured rosettes and birds.

sections.heading: Maharashtra- Handicrafts- Tusser Silks
sections.content: Ganeshpur in Bhandara district is famous for tusser silk weaving. It is the main occupation of the Koshti community which is half the working population of this district. They claim to be descendents of sage Makaranda known to have woven the first fabric from lotus fibre to clothe the gods. Tusser silk produced here is known by its Sanskrit name kosa. Some varieties of tusser silk produced in this area are motha choukada - a design in big squares, lahan choukada - a design in small squares, gunja salai - diagonal designs on cloth along with coloured lines at regular intervals in green, blue or orange, teen dhari choukada -- the three square pattern, and rasta choukada -- square pattern with horizontal lines running through.

sections.heading: Maharashtra- Handicrafts-Weaving- Mashru and Himru
sections.content: Aurangabad is famous for Mashru and Himru fabrics. These two types of fabrics are made of cotton and silk having a shine like satin. The ornamental design is formed on the principle of extra weft figuring. The extra silk weft left loose makes the Himru shawl soft, which almost feels like silk. Weavers were brought to Aurangabad from Banaras and Ahmedabad by Mohamed-bin-Tughlak and thus the Himru industry started.

sections.heading: Interesting Facts
sections.content: Mumbai is a major center of the Indian film industry being the largest in the world producing over 1200 films each year. The industry is supported mainly by a vast film-going Indian public, though Indian films have been gaining popularity in the rest of the world. Cinema first came to India in 1896, when the Lumiere Brothers' Cinematographe showed six short films in the Watson Hotel in Bombay. Three years later Harishchandra Bhatvadekar shot and exhibited two short films. Following that, there were several attempts to film stage plays and imported films were shown in the first decade of the twentieth century. The first indigenous silent feature film was Raja Harishchandra, released in 1913 and directed by Dhundiraj Govind Phalke, nicknamed "Dadasaheb," who is known as the father of Indian films. Bollywood is the informal name given to the popular Mumbai-based Hindi film industry in India. The name is a combination of Bombay, the old name of Mumbai, and Hollywood, the center of the United States film industry.

sections.heading: Maharashtra- Fairs and Festivals - Ganesh Chaturthi
sections.content: Also known as Vinayak Chaturthi, Ganesh Chaturthi is a festival celebrating the day on which Lord Ganesh, son of Shiva and Parvati appeared on earth for his devotees. According to the Hindu calendar, Ganesh Chaturthi is celebrated on the Shukla Chaturthi which is usually between 20 August and 15 September. The festival lasts for almost 10 days. The festival commences with the installation of the idol of Ganesh in beautifully decorated pandals. The pandals are decorated with paintings depicting the life of Lord Ganesha. The festival also includes a lot of cultural activities like music and dance. A popular sweet made during the Ganesh Chaturthi are modak and karanjis which are sweets made of coconut, jaggery, and other flavors.

sections.heading: Maharashtra- Fairs and Festivals- Parsi New Year
sections.content: The Parsi New Year is also known as Navroze and is mainly celebrated by a particular sect of Parsis, the Faslis. It is also celebrated by the Muslims of Iran and Zoroastrians. Navroze is the first day of the first month according to the Zoroastrian calendar. Originally an agricultural festival, the Parsi New Year later transformed into a religious festival. The day is celebrated by wearing new and colorful clothes, decorating the house with colours, lighting incense sticks and sprinkling sandalwood powder on live coal. The day begins by going to the Fire Temple and offering Jashan or a thanksgiving prayer service and offering sandalwood to the holy fire. Food is a significant part of the Parsi New Year. It includes a wide selection of non-vegetarian dishes, fruits and nuts. Two important dishes in breakfast for the Parsi New Year are Ravo and fried vermicelli cooked in sugar syrup and decorated with raisins.

sections.heading: Maharashtra- Performing Art- Dance- Tamasha
sections.content: Tamasha is a form of theatre, which came into existence in the early sixteenth century in Maharashtra, which includes the love songs i.e. lavanis due to which, this folk art, was very popular among the common people. Lavani is a combination of traditional song and dance, performed by women. It is performed to the beats of dholak. The word lavani originates from lavanya, meaning beauty. Earlier, this art form dealt with different and varied subject matters such as society, religion, politics, romance, etc. It is said that Lavani was used as a form of entertainment and morale booster to the tired soldiers during the eighteenth and nineteenth century Maratha battle. Many famous Marathi poets like Honaji Bala, Ramjoshi, Prabhakar, have written for Lavani.

sections.heading: Maharashtra- Performing Art- Dance- Koli
sections.content: Koli is one of the most popular folk dance forms of Maharashtra that derives its name from the fisher folk known as Kolis. It is a dance of joy, which is a celebration of valuable life, performed with sheer exuberance by the dancers. Both men and women in groups perform these dances, where all the performers have to make a single row or stand in pairs and portray many fishing actions in the dance form, by holding small oars in their hands and moving those to the beats of the songs. Generally, women participants wear green coloured sarees in their Koli style, whose length comes upto their knees; while the men wear a lungi having a triangular shape. The dance sequences include actions like rowing of a boat, or movement of waves, where swaying of oars in backward and forward direction creates a scene of a boat tossing on the high sea-waves. Ellora is the finest example of cave temples with almost thirty four caves with intricate interiors and ornamental facades. Carved during the 350 CE and 700 CE, the rock temples and monasteries represent three faiths - Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism. Cave 10, a Chaitya-hall is popularly known as Visvakarma' with a seated Buddha in a stupa. The Ramesvara cave has figurines of river goddesses adorning its entrance. The Dumar Lena cave is dedicated to Lord Shiva. Among the viharas, Cave 5 is the largest. The most impressive vihara is the three - storeyed cave called 'Tin - Tala'. The Kailasa temple in cave 16 is a masterpiece in itself. The temple that took nearly hundred years to be completed is decorated with themes and incidents from the puranas. Consisting of exquisite carvings, the cave temple is the most striking one amongst the other 30 at the site. Though carved out of one single rock, the temple looks like a freestanding structural southern type temple. The exterior of the temple is richly carved with niches, plasters, windows as well as images of deities, mithunas (erotic male and female figures) and other figures. Most of the deities at the left of the entrance are Shaivaite (followers of Lord Shiva) while on the right hand side the deities are Vaishnavites (followers of Lord Vishnu). The whole temple consists of a shrine with a ling at the rear of the hall with a Dravidian shikhara, a flat-roofed mandapa supported by sixteen pillars, a separate porch for Nandi surrounded by an open-court entered through a low gopuram. There are two Dhvajastambhas Ajanta Photo Gallery (pillars with the flagstaff) in the courtyard. The grand sculpture of Ravana attempting to lift mount Kailasa, the abode of Lord Shiva, with his full might is a landmark in Indian art. All the carvings are done in more than one level. The lower storey consists of several large shrines while the gallery along the three sides at the rear contains huge sculpted panels. A two-storeyed gateway on the west side provides access to the main temple and the Nandi mandapa, both on the same level, and is approximately seven meters high. The lower storey of the main temple as well as the Nandi shrine is solid but unaccessible. Stone bridges carved from the living rock connect the Nandi pavilion and the entrance porch of the temple. The main temple has a southern style superstructure. The lower storey has almost life-size elephants carved as if they are holding up the temple. The Jaina Caves (30 to 34) are massive, well-proportioned, decorated and mark the last phase of the activity at Ellora.
